title: British Typhoons Flew a French Nuclear Strike Profile for the First Time — and Doha Started Buying Into Weapons Design
subhead: Exercise Rummy put RAF jets on a simulated French nuclear mission over the Mediterranean, while Qatar said it wants to co-design weapons rather than just buy them. Both point the same direction: allies are hedging against U.S. guarantees rather than waiting on them.

sections.heading: France and Britain Fly a Joint Nuclear Strike Mission for the First Time
sections.body:
French Rafale jets carrying simulated nuclear-tipped cruise missiles flew alongside RAF Eurofighter Typhoons over the Mediterranean on Oct. 20-21 during exercise Rummy, the first joint airborne nuclear-strike drill between the two countries, the French Armed Forces Ministry said Friday (Defense News). No live weapons were involved. The aircraft launched from Saint-Dizier air base in northeastern France, supported by A330 MRTT tankers.

The mission implements the Northwood Declaration signed in July 2025, in which London and Paris agreed to deepen nuclear coordination and stated that no extreme threat to Europe would go unanswered by both nations. French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin framed it as coordination without integration: 'Having independent nuclear forces doesn't exclude coordination.'

French Armed Forces Chief of Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said crews demonstrated 'a very high level of interoperability.' Analyst Etienne Marcuz of the Fondation pour la Recherche Strategique called the participation of at least three British Typhoons 'quite significant' and a 'revolution' for the Strategic Air Forces, which had operated in total autonomy since the 1960s.

The political context is U.S. uncertainty. France is pitching a 'forward deterrence' concept to European allies, and the UK lacks an airborne nuclear leg entirely — its deterrent is submarine-only. French pilots are also set to start training Ukrainians on Rafale in November.
sections.whyItMatters: Britain has no air-launched nuclear weapon of its own, so this exercise is really about whether France's airborne leg can be presented as a European asset. That is a political offer as much as a military one, and it gets more credible each time a British squadron flies the mission profile.

sections.heading: Qatar Wants to Be a Weapons Designer, Not Just a Buyer
sections.body:
Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatari Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Affairs Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said the country is exploring new defense partnerships with the UK and others and wants to build a domestic weapons-production hub, Defense One reported. Priorities from a 2025 defense review: air defense, counter-drone systems, cybersecurity and electronic warfare.

Maj. Gen. Mohammed Abdul Latif Al Mannai said a UK partnership could feed Qatari operational requirements and threat assessments directly into weapons development. British Army Chief of the General Staff Gen. Sir Roly Walker described 'high-level political ambition for a 50-year strategic partnership,' adding that the UK wants to act 'almost as a design partner.' Barzan Holdings CEO Mohammed bin Badr Al Sada said British companies are already in Doha discussing the hub.

The driver is the collapse of the assumption that hosting U.S. troops equals protection. Israel struck Doha in September 2025, and Iran's June 2025 missile attack on Al Udeid Air Base — home to the largest U.S. military facility in the region — showed the base itself is a target. Qatar has also faced congressional friction: Sen. Chris Murphy said in October the Pentagon barred him from visiting Al Udeid, which he called a cover-up of war damage (Defense News).

Defense One noted Milipol Qatar looked more like a banking expo than an arms fair, a reminder that Qatar has no real manufacturing base to build on.
sections.whyItMatters: Every Gulf state is now pricing in the possibility that the U.S. umbrella is conditional. Qatar's answer is equity and co-design rather than shopping — a model the UK badly needs export revenue for, and one that would put Gulf money inside European supply chains.

sections.heading: A Russian Satellite Shadowed a Ukraine-Linked Radar Satellite at One-Third of a Mile
sections.body:
The U.S. accused Russia at the UN of deliberately maneuvering Cosmos 2612 close to ICEYE-X36, a radar satellite operated by the U.S. arm of Finland's ICEYE that supplies imagery to Ukraine's military, Defense News reported. The Russian satellite spent over two weeks closing in, then held station as close as one-third of a mile over the weekend of Oct. 17, roughly 345 miles up.

Undersecretary of State Thomas G. DiNanno called the behavior 'threatening' and 'consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.' Space historian Jonathan McDowell said he believed it was the first rendezvous in low Earth orbit between two active satellites without one owner's approval.

At the CSIS panel on the encounter, Clayton Swope of the Aerospace Security Project described the logic plainly: Russia wants to 'poke the West in the eye and watch the West do nothing.' Greg Gillinger of Integrity ISR noted both objects travel at roughly 4 miles per second, making a one-kilometer approach 'the equivalent of flying in a very tight formation.'

This lands weeks after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly confirmed the U.S. has weapons in orbit, and after the Space Force picked two companies to build space-to-space reconnaissance satellites by 2028. On Oct. 23, China published a new outer space position paper warning against a space arms race (SCMP).
sections.whyItMatters: Commercial satellites now carry the imagery and connectivity militaries fight with, and they are not defended like military assets. Russia demonstrated it can park next to one for days without consequence. The response gap is the story — the U.S. is willing to say it has orbital weapons but not to use them for a commercial escort mission.

sections.heading: Leonardo and Rheinmetall Close In on $4.16B of Italian Armor
sections.body:
The Leonardo-Rheinmetall 50-50 joint venture has secured two contracts with the Italian Army worth $4.16 billion for A2CS combat vehicles and a new-generation main battle tank, Italian financial daily MF reported (via Defense News). Rheinmetall declined to comment, and Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani said he could not confirm signature because communications must be coordinated with the client — a notable gap between the reported deal and official confirmation.

Mariani said the program is 'ready to enter production from our side,' with work progressing on both the tank and the Future Combat System in cooperation with Rheinmetall. He stressed the importance of the tank line for Italy's own modernization and for exports. The JV was launched in 2024.

Earlier in the week, the Pentagon and BAE Systems signed a framework agreement for up to 25,000 APKWS guidance kits per year, converting unguided rockets into precision munitions — cheap, fast, high-volume production rather than exquisite systems.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Europe's land-industry consolidation finally producing orders. The export framing matters: the Leonardo-Rheinmetall tank is being built with a third-party customer in mind, which is how European primes intend to survive the post-2030 spending plateau.

sections.heading: Petraeus: No NATO Military Has Begun the Reorganization Drone War Requires
sections.body:
Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia's casualties on the Ukrainian front line, and no NATO military — including the U.S. — has begun the institutional overhaul that implies, retired Gen. David Petraeus said at a Washington event, per Defense News. Ukraine and Russia each fly roughly 10,000 drones a day, he estimated. 'Tanks aren't survivable there anymore,' he said.

Petraeus praised the Pentagon's new Autonomous Warfare Command, announced by Defense Secretary Hegseth in late September as a four-star command requiring each service to stand up a component. But he warned against creating a force structure without changing how the Pentagon buys: the goal should be 'very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time,' with software changes weekly and hardware every few weeks.

He also acknowledged the interceptor drain from the U.S. war with Iran: a Congressional Budget Office estimate cited by Defense News put U.S. consumption at between one-half and two-thirds of certain missile-defense interceptor inventories.

Separately, Defense One reported the Netherlands is designing a different procurement model — paying commercial firms to stay on call so they can switch from making cars to drones when a conflict breaks out. Procurement minister Derk Boswijk: 'We can buy 1 million drones, but I know one thing for sure: that weeks from now they are outdated.'
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between recognizing drone dominance and reorganizing to exploit it is now the central procurement problem in the West. Petraeus's number — 90% of casualties — is the argument that makes legacy armor and manned aviation budgets politically vulnerable.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Is Expanding a Missile Plant That Relies on Chinese Technology
sections.body:
Satellite imagery of the al-Duwadimi complex about 125 miles west of Riyadh, taken by Planet Labs between April 2025 and September 2026, shows a new building housing casting pits at least twice the size of the existing one, according to researchers Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute. Their assessment, reported by Defense News, is that the expansion is likely for larger solid-fuel missiles with longer range or heavier payloads.

FPRI, IISS and CNA analysts told Reuters that the complex's characteristics point to Chinese technology. Saudi Arabia secretly bought about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 missiles from China in 1987 per a declassified 1991 CIA estimate. Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, with the expansion aimed at the longer-range DF-21 class. Riyadh turned to Beijing because Washington restricts longer-range exports.

The blast walls around the new building — designed to protect nearby structures from accidental detonation — are themselves a signal of larger motor work. The Saudi embassy and information ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
sections.whyItMatters: A Saudi solid-fuel line with Chinese lineage changes the Gulf missile balance and complicates the pending U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement. It is also a quiet data point on Chinese proliferation reach into the Gulf, well beyond the Asia-Pacific focus of most coverage.

sections.heading: Liaoning Deployment Patterns, Ukraine's NSPA Access, and AI in the Tanker Fleet
sections.body:
China's first carrier, CNS Liaoning, is on its second far-seas deployment and by Oct. 23 was drilling near Japan's southernmost islands before heading toward the South China Sea near the Philippines, per East Asian media cited by Defense News. It sailed with two large destroyers and a guided-missile destroyer on Oct. 14. Analysts Carl Thayer and Collin Koh described the pattern as routine training designed to validate technology for the newer Shandong and Fujian, with Liaoning unlikely to be the front-line carrier in a contingency.

Ukraine will be able to buy weapons and equipment through NATO's NSPA centralized procurement agency, the Financial Times reported — potentially faster and cheaper access to allied industrial base. It comes amid damaged U.S.-Ukraine relations after Trump's diesel export deal with Russia, though Zelensky said an Oslo meeting on Tuesday agreed to resolve Starshield and intelligence-sharing issues.

The U.S. Air Force issued an SBIR solicitation (deadline Nov. 25) for AI to analyze aerial refueling from tanker-mounted cameras and generate automated 'hot wash' feedback for KC-46 crews, aiming to cut human bias in one of aviation's most demanding tasks. Also this week: an F-22 pilot flew an Anduril FQ-44 Collaborative Combat Aircraft as an airborne 'quarterback,' and South Korea's Hanwha demonstrated laser weapons downing three drones in a Republic of Korea Army exercise.
sections.whyItMatters: Liaoning's voyages are about generating trained carrier crews, not signaling. Ukraine joining NSPA is the more consequential item: it starts moving Kyiv's supply relationships from bilateral U.S. dependency toward the European industrial base.

bottomLine: The week's most telling defense developments were about dependency, not firepower. France and Britain demonstrated that Europe's two nuclear forces can operate in the same mission profile, even though only one of them has an air-launched weapon. Qatar said it wants equity in weapons programs precisely because hosting U.S. troops did not stop Iranian missiles from hitting Al Udeid. Ukraine gained access to NATO's procurement agency while its U.S. supply line wobbles. Meanwhile a Russian satellite sat a third of a mile from a commercial radar satellite feeding Ukrainian targeting data, and Washington's response was a UN complaint. On the industrial side, the Leonardo-Rheinmetall JV moved toward $4.16 billion in Italian armor orders and Saudi Arabia expanded a Chinese-derived solid-fuel missile plant. The through-line is that the postwar assumption of buying security from a single supplier is being replaced — unevenly, expensively, and with considerable technical dependence on China in the Gulf.
sources: Defense News, Defense One, Financial Times (via Defense News), Reuters (via Defense News), Foreign Policy Research Institute, IISS, CNA, CSIS Aerospace Security Project, Fondation pour la Recherche Strategique, South China Morning Post, Xinhua, Global Times, Congressional Budget Office
